questions.stem: Four hours after a percutaneous kidney biopsy, a client reports new flank pain on the biopsy side. The urine in the collection bag has turned from pink to bright red with clots. Heart rate has risen from 82 to 118/min, and blood pressure has fallen from 136/80 to 98/60 mm Hg. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Keep the client on bed rest and prepare IV fluids and blood as prescribed
Help the client walk to the bathroom to empty the bladder
Give ibuprofen for the flank pain
Irrigate the catheter forcefully to clear the clots

parameters.text: Blood pressure, heart rate and hemoglobin
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Body weight measured once a week

rationale.correct: After kidney biopsy, watch for bleeding: hematuria with clots, flank pain, tachycardia and hypotension; keep the client on bed rest and notify the provider.

perOption.c1: Bright red urine with clots, flank pain, tachycardia and falling blood pressure after kidney biopsy point to hemorrhage.
perOption.c2: Infection develops over days with fever, not sudden hemodynamic change.
perOption.c3: The timing after biopsy and the falling blood pressure point to bleeding.
perOption.c4: Mild pink urine is expected; bright red urine with clots and shock is not.
perOption.a1: Bleeding may need imaging, transfusion or embolization.
perOption.a2: Bed rest limits bleeding, and volume support treats shock.
perOption.a5: Forceful irrigation is not done without a prescription.
perOption.p1: Show the extent of blood loss.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: During orientation on a busy step-down unit, a nurse is teaching new staff about the limits of pulse oximetry. For each situation, indicate how the SpO2 reading is most likely affected.

rows.text: A client with very cold fingers and poor circulation
A client with carbon monoxide poisoning
A client with warm hands and a good waveform
A client with dark nail polish on the probe finger

columns.text: May read falsely low or fail to read
May read falsely normal or high

rationale.correct: Pulse oximetry is unreliable with poor perfusion, motion, some nail polish and carbon monoxide; check the waveform and correlate with the client.

perOption.r1:c1: Poor blood flow weakens the signal.
perOption.r2:c2: Carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated hemoglobin.
perOption.r3:c1: No reason for a low reading.
perOption.r3:c2: No reason for a high reading.
perOption.r3:c3: Good perfusion and waveform give a reliable reading.
perOption.r4:c1: Some polish colors can interfere and give low or failed readings.

questions.stem: The nurse is measuring orthostatic vital signs for a client who feels dizzy when standing. Place the steps in order.

items.text: Help the client sit up and measure again after 1 to 2 minutes
Measure blood pressure and pulse after 1 and 3 minutes of standing
Have the client lie flat for at least 5 minutes, then measure blood pressure and pulse
Help the client stand, staying close to prevent a fall

rationale.correct: Orthostatic vital signs: lying for 5 minutes, then sitting and standing measurements; a systolic drop of 20 or diastolic drop of 10 mm Hg is positive.

questions.stem: A client is on the first night after a lumbar spinal fusion. Which assessments should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Movement, sensation and circulation in both legs
Surgical drain output and the dressing
Ability to void after the catheter is removed
Pain level and response to analgesia
Logrolling the client with the spine kept straight
Bending at the waist to check the back dressing

rationale.correct: After spinal fusion: neurovascular checks, drain and dressing, voiding, pain and logrolling to protect the spine.

perOption.b: Detects bleeding or a CSF leak.
perOption.c: Urinary retention is common after spinal surgery.
perOption.d: Guides pain control and early movement.
perOption.f: Twisting and bending stress the fusion.

questions.stem: A client with vomiting for 3 days has a BUN of 48 mg/dL and a creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL (ratio about 34). Urine is dark and scant. How should the nurse interpret these results?

options.text: Intrinsic kidney damage from a toxic drug
Dehydration that is reducing kidney blood flow
Normal results for an older adult after illness
A urinary blockage from an enlarged prostate

rationale.correct: A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20 suggests a prerenal cause such as dehydration, GI bleeding or high protein intake.

perOption.a: Intrinsic injury usually raises BUN and creatinine together, with a ratio closer to 10 to 15.
perOption.b: A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20 with dark, scant urine suggests a prerenal cause such as dehydration.
perOption.d: Obstruction is less likely with vomiting and dark urine.

questions.stem: A peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) was just placed at the bedside by the IV team. The provider has prescribed IV antibiotics to start now. What should the nurse do before using the PICC?

options.text: Flush it with saline and start the antibiotic right away
Confirm the tip position by x-ray or per policy
Check that blood can be drawn back easily, then start the infusion
Wait 24 hours to let the insertion site heal

rationale.correct: Confirm central line tip placement (x-ray or ECG-guided method per policy) before first use.

perOption.a: The tip position must be confirmed first.
perOption.b: The tip must be confirmed in the correct position before the line is used.
perOption.c: Blood return does not confirm tip location.
perOption.d: Waiting is not needed once placement is confirmed.

questions.stem: A client is going home with a 48-hour Holter monitor to find the cause of palpitations. Complete the sentences about the teaching.

content.template: The client should {{b1}} while wearing the monitor, keep a diary of {{b2}} and {{b3}} until it is removed.

options.text: carry out normal daily activities
stay in bed and rest
exercise as hard as possible
symptoms and activities with the times they happened
everything they eat
their weight each hour
avoid showering or getting the device wet
remove the electrodes at night
unplug it when they feel well

rationale.correct: Holter monitor teaching: normal activities, a symptom diary with times and keeping the device dry.

perOption.b1:a: The goal is to record the heart during usual activities.
perOption.b1:b: Rest would not show what triggers symptoms.
perOption.b2:a: The diary links symptoms with the recording.

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis has had an upper respiratory infection for 3 days. Today the client's speech is slurred, the eyelids droop more, the client chokes on sips of water and says it is hard to breathe. Vital capacity has fallen from 2.4 L to 1.1 L. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Prepare to support breathing, including possible intubation
Keep the client NPO and position upright with suction ready
Give a large meal to keep up the client's strength
Encourage the client to walk to build strength
Give a sedative to ease anxiety about breathing

parameters.text: Vital capacity and negative inspiratory force
Swallowing and ability to handle secretions
Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Body weight measured once a week

rationale.correct: Myasthenic crisis can cause respiratory failure; monitor vital capacity, protect the airway and prepare for ventilation and treatments such as IVIG or plasmapheresis.

perOption.c1: Worsening weakness with breathing and swallowing difficulty after an infection is myasthenic crisis.
perOption.c2: Cholinergic crisis follows too much medication and causes drooling, cramps and small pupils.
perOption.c3: GBS causes ascending paralysis, not worsening of known myasthenia.
perOption.c4: There are no focal deficits on one side.
perOption.p1: Falling values signal impending respiratory failure.

questions.stem: For each arterial blood gas, indicate the acid-base disorder.

rows.text: pH 7.28, PaCO2 58, HCO3 25 in a client with an opioid overdose
pH 7.51, PaCO2 28, HCO3 23 in an anxious client breathing fast
pH 7.22, PaCO2 30, HCO3 12 in a client with DKA
pH 7.52, PaCO2 46, HCO3 36 in a client with prolonged vomiting

rationale.correct: Match pH with the system that moved the same direction: CO2 opposite to pH means respiratory; HCO3 in the same direction as pH means metabolic.

perOption.r3:c3: Low pH with low HCO3; CO2 is falling to compensate.

questions.stem: A client admitted with Guillain-Barré syndrome had leg weakness 2 days ago. Today the weakness has spread to the arms and chest, and the client's voice is softer. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Checking the deep tendon reflexes in the legs
Measuring vital capacity and breathing effort
Testing the client's ability to walk in the hall
Measuring the client's calf circumference on both legs

rationale.correct: Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause respiratory failure as weakness ascends; monitor vital capacity and be ready for ventilation.

perOption.a: Reflexes are already expected to be reduced; breathing is the priority.
perOption.b: Ascending weakness can reach the breathing muscles; falling vital capacity signals the need for ventilation.
perOption.c: Walking is unsafe and not the priority.
perOption.d: DVT risk matters but is not the priority.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old client 3 days after a myocardial infarction treated with a stent reports sharp chest pain that gets worse when lying flat or breathing deeply and eases when leaning forward. The nurse hears a scratchy sound over the heart. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: A new myocardial infarction
Pericarditis after the infarction
A pulmonary embolism
Gastroesophageal reflux

rationale.correct: Pericarditis: sharp, positional chest pain relieved by leaning forward and a pericardial friction rub; watch for tamponade.

perOption.a: Pain from ischemia does not usually change with position.
perOption.b: Positional, pleuritic chest pain eased by leaning forward with a friction rub suggests pericarditis.
perOption.c: PE causes pleuritic pain and hypoxemia, but not a rub that changes with position.
perOption.d: Reflux does not cause a friction rub.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A client with myasthenia gravis takes pyridostigmine. Which statement shows correct understanding of when to take it?

options.text: "I'll take it at bedtime so it can work while I'm asleep."
"I'll take it 30 to 60 minutes before each of my meals."
"I'll take it when I feel very weak and tired during the day."
"I'll take extra doses if I feel stronger so I stay that way."

rationale.correct: Pyridostigmine is taken on schedule, about 30 to 60 minutes before meals, without extra doses.

perOption.a: Doses are timed to cover activities and meals.
perOption.b: Timing doses before meals improves chewing and swallowing.
perOption.d: Extra doses can cause cholinergic crisis.

segments.text: deep, fast breathing and fruity breath

rationale.correct: Drowsiness, Kussmaul breathing, severe acidosis and poor perfusion show severe DKA in a child.

perOption.s2: Changed alertness in DKA can signal worsening acidosis or cerebral edema.
perOption.s4: Kussmaul breathing and ketone odor show severe ketoacidosis.
perOption.s6: Explains the new diagnosis but is not an immediate threat.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the child's data.

content.template: The child has new-onset type 1 diabetes presenting as {{b1}}, and the high potassium is most likely {{b2}}.

options.text: severe diabetic ketoacidosis
hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
gastroenteritis
a shift of potassium out of cells, hiding a total-body deficit
a sign of too much potassium in the diet
a reason to restrict potassium during treatment

rationale.correct: In DKA, serum potassium may be high despite a total-body deficit; it falls with insulin and fluids and needs close monitoring and replacement.

perOption.b1:a: High glucose, pH 7.12, low bicarbonate and high ketones show severe DKA.
perOption.b1:b: HHS lacks significant acidosis and ketones.
perOption.b1:c: The glucose and acidosis point to DKA.
perOption.b2:a: Acidosis and lack of insulin move potassium out of cells; total-body potassium is low.
perOption.b2:c: Potassium usually falls quickly with insulin and must be replaced.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: For each complication of treatment, indicate whether the child is at high or low risk.

rows.text: Cerebral edema
Hypokalemia as insulin starts
Hypoglycemia if dextrose is not added as glucose falls
Hypertensive crisis

rationale.correct: Pediatric DKA treatment risks include cerebral edema, hypokalemia and hypoglycemia.

perOption.r1:c1: Children with severe DKA, especially new-onset, are at highest risk.
perOption.r2:c1: Insulin moves potassium into cells, so levels can drop quickly.
perOption.r4:c1: The child is dehydrated with low-normal blood pressure.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize risks during pediatric DKA treatment.

questions.stem: Which monitoring should the nurse include during the first hours of treatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Glucose every hour
Neurological checks every hour, watching for headache or a falling level of consciousness
Electrolytes, including potassium, every 2 to 4 hours
Strict intake and output
Body weight measured once each week
Oral fluids as much as the child wants while vomiting

rationale.correct: Pediatric DKA monitoring: hourly glucose and neurological checks, frequent electrolytes and strict intake and output.

perOption.f: The child is vomiting; fluids are given IV.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: Which plan for insulin should the nurse expect for this child?

options.text: A large IV insulin bolus followed by an infusion
A low-dose IV insulin infusion after fluids, with no bolus
Subcutaneous long-acting insulin given once a day
Insulin by mouth with small sips of clear fluid

rationale.correct: In pediatric DKA, start a low-dose continuous insulin infusion after initial fluid replacement, without a bolus, and correct slowly.

perOption.a: Insulin boluses are avoided in children because of cerebral edema risk.
perOption.b: Pediatric DKA uses a continuous infusion (about 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hr) after fluids begin, with no bolus.
perOption.c: IV insulin is needed for severe DKA.

questions.stem: Six hours into treatment, the nurse reassesses the child. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs immediate action.

rows.text: Glucose 260 mg/dL and falling about 70 mg/dL per hour
pH 7.24 and bicarbonate 13 mEq/L
New severe headache, slowing heart rate and confusion
Breathing slower and less deep

perOption.r1:c1: A steady fall is the goal.
perOption.r4:c1: Kussmaul breathing eases as acidosis improves.

perOption.r2: Bradycardia is common with inferior MI and may need treatment.
perOption.r3: Low blood pressure affects drug choices and suggests possible right ventricular involvement.
perOption.r4: Oxygen is not needed at this saturation.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues in an inferior STEMI.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client is having an {{b1}}, which most often involves blockage of the {{b2}}.

options.text: inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction
anterior STEMI
unstable angina
right coronary artery
left anterior descending artery
pulmonary artery

rationale.correct: Inferior STEMI usually involves the right coronary artery and can cause bradycardia and right ventricular infarction.

perOption.b1:a: ST elevation in II, III and aVF shows an inferior STEMI.
perOption.b1:b: Anterior STEMI shows changes in V1 to V4.
perOption.b2:a: The right coronary artery usually supplies the inferior wall and the SA and AV nodes.
perOption.b2:b: The LAD supplies the anterior wall.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Inferior STEMI with possible right ventricular involvement

actions.text: Activate the cath lab team for emergency reperfusion
Give aspirin to chew as prescribed
Give sublingual nitroglycerin for the chest pain
Give a large dose of furosemide
Wait for troponin results before calling the cath lab

parameters.text: Bowel sounds in each of the four quadrants
Body weight measured once a week

rationale.correct: STEMI: rapid reperfusion and aspirin; avoid nitrates after PDE-5 inhibitors and with hypotension or right ventricular infarction; monitor rhythm, pressure and pain.

perOption.c1: ST elevation in the inferior leads with hypotension points to inferior STEMI that may involve the right ventricle.
perOption.c2: Pain lasting 40 minutes with ST elevation is infarction.
perOption.c3: Tearing pain to the back and unequal pulses would suggest dissection.
perOption.c4: Pericarditis causes diffuse ST changes and positional pain.
perOption.a1: STEMI needs reperfusion as soon as possible.
perOption.a3: Nitrates are contraindicated after sildenafil and with hypotension.
perOption.a4: Diuresis would worsen hypotension, especially with right ventricular involvement.
perOption.a5: STEMI treatment does not wait for troponin.
perOption.p1: Bradycardia, heart block and hypotension are common.

references: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize care in an inferior STEMI.

questions.stem: After a stent is placed through the right femoral artery, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the groin site for bleeding or a hematoma
Check pulses, color and temperature of the right leg
Keep the right leg straight for the prescribed time
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees right away
Watch the telemetry for rhythm changes
Have the client walk within the first hour

rationale.correct: After femoral PCI: check the site, distal pulses and the leg, keep the leg straight and monitor rhythm.

perOption.a: Bleeding is the most common complication.
perOption.d: Bending the hip can cause bleeding.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Care for a client after femoral PCI.

questions.stem: The client still has chest pain while waiting for the cath lab. The provider is considering pain relief. Which statement by the nurse is most important to share?

options.text: "The client is anxious and asking for something to help them calm down."
"The client took sildenafil last night; BP is 98/62."
"The client would like ice chips for a dry mouth."
"The client's spouse is on the way to the hospital."

rationale.correct: Before nitrates, check for PDE-5 inhibitor use (sildenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours), hypotension and right ventricular infarction.

perOption.a: Useful, but not the key safety issue.
perOption.b: Nitrates with recent sildenafil and low blood pressure can cause severe hypotension.

exhibits.title: Pediatric emergency department, 0900
exhibits.body: A 9-year-old with no known history of diabetes has had increased thirst, frequent urination and weight loss for 3 weeks. Since last night the child has vomited three times and has abdominal pain. The child is drowsy but answers questions, breathing is deep and fast and the breath smells fruity.

exhibits.title: Emergency department, 0615
exhibits.body: A 61-year-old client has had crushing chest pain spreading to the jaw for 40 minutes, with nausea and sweating. History: hypertension, smoking and erectile dysfunction treated with sildenafil, last taken last night. The 12-lead ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF.
